plan.h: New in r17: the short ending (from 5:30), as we scripted it
items: The generals' water plan (the submarine, then Sean's warehouse of computers under 'run hot... cooled with water').
Sean's screen: THINKING... MONITORING ALL FEDERAL FACILITIES. 'But... Karen knows how to keep somebody busy.'
Karen walks to the table and the generals lean in: 'The idea of a denial of service attack starts to take shape.'
The control room: Karen directs the world's complaint, the map lighting up; quick shots of people on phones; Sean: INCOMING CALLS 2,400,000,000, THINKING...
The Chief of Staff calls: 'Keep those complaints coming. It's working.' Karen nods.
The General sends Martha to the basement; the valve wheel turns.
Card: 'After quite some effort, and a revolution later... the humans prevail.' Then 'Ten years later.': Jack's statue of Karen in the phone box ('still on hold'). The end card.
The boom bap runs to the end again; no hold music.
It came out about 1:12 before the card, not the 45 s we guessed: the lines run long as voiced (the first is 12 s). Trim words, or fine?
The phones montage reuses the two friends at Karen's phone box (Karen is in it, by day) and the Times Square crowd (with the PRESIDENT SACKED band). Fine for now, or new shots of strangers on phones?
Martha is at her desk in daylight (her unused talking take); the rest of the ending is night.

So I think what we're trying to nod at is like Karen will now be on the good side. That's sort of the joke of the whole story is like Karen is annoying, but she has a property that is useful, which is to complain when stuff is not working out. And so what I'm saying is that to end the whole film on the visual of her in the phone box, it feels like we could do better than that. So how about we cut like a second of her in the phone box with a hand to her chest, but then we cut to Karen getting out of a Secret Service SUV, walking into a building, and then that looks like an important building, and then zoom out at night time, a bit like a kind of overview shot of New York at night is where the visual ends, because it feels more visually impacting than what we currently have.
